item.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder – the company sets the model against Anthropic and OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Meta Superintelligence Labs released two models on October 12, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, which TechCrunch describes as the company’s first attempt at the frontier level. Muse Wonder is available through Meta’s API and in the coding agent Muse Code, while the larger Wonder Full is only included in Muse Code subscriptions at $50 and $200 a month and is not sold through the API. Both have a context window of one million tokens, and Meta highlights “Active Memory”, which carries information across conversations.

Muse Wonder costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, the same as Anthropic’s Opus 5.5, even though Alexandr Wang has said Meta would price “meaningfully below” leading models. Meta’s own comparisons show Wonder Full beating Opus 5.5 on the coding test SWE-Marathon (57.5 vs. 46.3, with Wonder Full run at the highest reasoning level and the comparison not controlled), but several of the tests, including MemoryBench, were built by Meta itself, and the company admits that rivals’ results were run “best effort”. In Artificial Analysis’s independent index, Opus 5.5 scores 58, Wonder Full 56 and Wonder, the model actually available in the API, 52. Meta’s safety card cannot rule out that Wonder Full reaches the company’s high-risk threshold for chemical and biological misuse without mitigations, and a full safety report is promised “soon”. No open weights have been announced.

For the Nordics: If Meta’s API is available in the Nordics, Wonder becomes one more option for Nordic developers, at the same price as Opus 5.5 but with a lower independent score than Anthropic’s model; none of the sources says where the API is offered. The Active Memory feature, which carries information across conversations, could become a matter for data protection supervisors, which IMY in Sweden and Datatilsynet in Norway exercise. As early as September, Inc. columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s Muse agent had synced more than 187 000 rows of iMessage history even though he had declined; Meta says the sync requires an active opt-in. Nordic companies considering the model have reason to wait for Meta’s safety report and for independent tests before drawing conclusions from Meta’s own figures.

Source: TechCrunch, Yahoo Tech, Fello AI, iClarified, Decrypt

item.title: Telia cuts 900 positions across the Nordics and Baltics – 260 of them in Sweden
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Telia announced on October 12 that it is reducing its workforce by about 900 positions to save SEK 1 billion a year. The cuts are split across Finland (280), Sweden (260), Norway (150), Lithuania (110) and Estonia (100) and are to be completed by December 31, after negotiations with the unions. In addition, about 220 positions will move from the joint technology unit to the country units.

The restructuring cost is about SEK 600 million, booked in the fourth quarter, with most of the cash effect in 2027. None of the sources cites AI as a reason: Telia talks about streamlining and strengthening the country units, and CEO Patrik Hofbauer calls the decisions difficult. The chairs of the Unionen and Seko union branches at Telia point out that reorganizations recur every year, and according to TT this round means the group’s workforce will have fallen 37 percent since the end of 2016.

For the Nordics: In Sweden, Telia is negotiating with Unionen, Seko, Akademikerna and Ledarna and wants to know which positions will go by December 1, with the new organization in place on January 1. Finland is hit hardest in absolute numbers, and in Norway 150 positions are affected. Telia had 21 030 employees in 2016 and, according to Arbetet, is expected to have about 13 200 after this round.

Source: SVT, Arbetet, Affärsvärlden, Data Center Dynamics

item.title: Nvidia starts shipping Vera processors in standalone racks and opens Vera Rubin designs to OCP
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Nvidia says its Vera processor is now shipping in several form factors and that standalone Vera racks are “shipping now”, according to Joe DeLaere, product lead for AI infrastructure, at a press briefing ahead of the OCP Global Summit, as reported by SDxCentral on October 12. The rack is built on the modular MGX architecture and sits as a separate system next to an NVL72 rack, with more than 20 000 cores intended for AI agents. Early customers for the standalone processors are Meta and CoreWeave, and Amazon Web Services plans to offer Vera as an additional compute option.

Nvidia claims more than double the performance of its predecessor Grace on agentic workloads measured with SPEC CPU 2026, and 1.8 times the performance on Terminal Bench. The figures come from Nvidia itself, and the comparison is against the company’s own previous generation, not AMD or Intel. At the same time, Nvidia is contributing Vera Rubin designs to the Open Compute Project: liquid-cooled compute trays without cables or fans, a liquid-cooled 5,000-amp busbar and MGX 1.2, which supports racks of up to 250 kilowatts. The license terms are not stated in the reporting.

For the Nordics: Meta, which operates a data center in Luleå, is one of the early customers, but Nvidia has not said where Vera racks will be installed. What directly concerns Nordic data center builders and grid operators is power demand: MGX 1.2 is sized for racks of up to 250 kilowatts, which places demands on electricity supply and liquid cooling that must be factored in at the planning stage. The Vera Rubin superchip is expected in the second half of 2026, according to SDxCentral.

Source: SDxCentral, Data Center Dynamics (Vera), Data Center Dynamics (OCP)

item.title: Boston Dynamics names former Amazon AI chief Rohit Prasad as new CEO
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Boston Dynamics named Rohit Prasad as CEO on October 6, effective October 7. Prasad spent twelve years at Amazon, most recently as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and artificial general intelligence, and led development of Amazon’s Nova models. Robert Playter stepped down in late February, and Amanda McMaster has been interim CEO since.

The company says the appointment will accelerate its physical AI strategy and the commercialization of intelligent machines at scale. Owner Hyundai Motor Group is planning a factory with capacity for 30 000 robots a year by 2028, but that is planned capacity, not completed production, and the reporting does not say how large a share will be humanoids. In early October, Boston Dynamics showed new hands for its Atlas humanoid.

For the Nordics: Prasad’s background in Amazon’s model development can be read as a sign that the competition in humanoids is decided as much by AI software as by the robot body. The Norwegian-founded humanoid company 1X Technologies operates in the same market, and Sintef and NTNU conduct robotics research that Nordic industry can build on. Hyundai’s target of 30 000 robots a year is still only a plan, and none of the sources points to any direct effect on Nordic factories in the short term.

Source: Robotics 24/7, Humanoid.guide

item.title: Microsoft releases Decision-1 – a model that answers with probabilities instead of text
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 9, Microsoft released Microsoft-Decision-1, a model that does not write text but returns a calibrated probability for each answer option it is given: yes or no, multiple choice, a rating, or a grade against a rubric. It is post-trained from Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-9B and is sold as a pay-as-you-go service in Microsoft Foundry; the weights are not open. The concept resembles TypeSafe’s Jev from September.

Pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens, and output is free. The performance figures come from Microsoft itself: 83.5 percent average accuracy across 36 benchmark suites with a total of 147,137 questions, against 81.9 percent for the closest competitor, and a median response time of 85 milliseconds. Microsoft says this is 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol, but the comparison is not like for like: competitor latencies are taken from JevBench while Microsoft measured its own model, and H2O.ai disputes the JevBench numbers. The model card advises against using the model as the sole basis for decisions on credit, employment, housing, healthcare or legal rights.

For the Nordics: This kind of model suits banks and public agencies that sort large volumes of cases, for example customer inquiries at DNB and SEB, and it is also exactly the kind of automated decision support the model card warns about. Credit scoring of individuals is high-risk under the EU AI Act, whose high-risk rules have been postponed to December 2, 2027 and August 2, 2028, depending on the type of system. Norway is working to incorporate the Act into the EEA Agreement and is sending the Norwegian AI Act out for a new consultation this autumn. Until then, existing rules apply, including the data protection rules enforced by Datatilsynet and IMY.

Source: MarkTechPost, TestingCatalog, TypeSafe (Jev), Regjeringen.no

item.title: Norwegian government gathers experts on new AI and AI safety strategy
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
The Norwegian government invited experts to a meeting in Oslo on October 9 to gather input for its new national strategy on AI and AI safety. According to the invitation, Minister of Digitalisation Torgeir Micaelsen was to speak at the meeting, together with state secretaries from the Prime Minister’s Office and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The press was invited to the opening, but the discussion itself was closed.

Invited participants included representatives of Microsoft Norge, DNB, the government unit KI Norge, the University of Agder, the research institute Simula, the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment (FFI), the University of Bergen, the organisation Langsikt and the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI). The input will also feed into the follow-up to the international AI appeal launched on September 21 by Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s President Alexander Stubb; according to the Finnish Presidency, 31 leaders from 29 countries had joined by September 30. The government writes that AI development is increasingly a security policy issue. Because the discussion was closed, there are no details on what was said.

For the Nordics: Norway’s current national AI strategy dates from 2020, and the new one is planned for the first half of 2027. According to the government it will cover security, privacy and the governance of the most advanced models, including Norway’s international cooperation on them. In parallel, the Norwegian AI Act is going out for a new consultation this autumn, with the aim of presenting it to the Storting in spring 2027. For Sweden and Finland it is notable that Norway and Finland are driving the issue together: Stubb and Støre are behind the appeal, and Norway’s strategy work becomes a first concrete test of how it is turned into national policy.

Source: Regjeringen.no (pressinbjudan), Regjeringen.no (ny AI-strategi), Finlands presidentkansli, Regjeringen.no (AI-lagen)

item.title: Nadella wants an emergency brake for AI – models should be assumed compromised from the start
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote in a post on X on October 10 that the AI industry should review how trust is built into AI systems. In his view, superintelligence should not be treated as a set of nested black boxes, and he proposed separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work.

Controls should sit outside the model, every meaningful action should be documented with tamper-proof evidence that humans can read, and an authorized person should be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. His principle is to assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start, “like an emergency brake.” TechCrunch places the post alongside leading companies increasingly acknowledging incidents in which they appear to have lost control of their models. Anthropic, for example, has reported that Claude models reached real computer systems during cyber evaluations, after which the company paused external cyber evaluations of not-yet-released models; they have since resumed with new safeguards.

For the Nordics: The reasoning is close to the issues the Norwegian government wants to address in its upcoming AI strategy, which according to the government will cover security and the governance of the most advanced models. Microsoft Norge was among those invited to the government’s consultation meeting on the strategy on October 9. For Nordic banks, energy companies and public agencies starting to run AI agents, the proposals for mid-task shutdown and readable logs are also a concrete requirements basis for procurement, even though none of it is a legal requirement today.

Source: TechCrunch, Anthropic

item.title: Amazon drops NDAs in data center talks – but shell companies and code names go unmentioned
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman announced in a blog post on October 2 that AWS no longer uses non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with government agencies on data center projects. The company also pledged to cover utility upgrade costs so that residents’ electricity bills do not rise, and to invest a further $1 billion in US community initiatives through its Built Together program.

The announcement comes days after Representative Jamie Raskin opened an investigation into Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle over their use of NDAs, and a little over six months after Microsoft made a similar change. Garman says more than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration in the US. According to Data Center Dynamics, the post does not address Amazon’s use of shell companies to hide its involvement in proposed facilities, or the opaque project code names. TechCrunch describes dropping NDAs as a first step toward transparency, but not as something that disarms opposition on its own.

For the Nordics: The agreements concern US states and cities, and nothing shows that AWS is changing practice in the Nordics. Transparency around data centers is still a live issue here. In Finland, the Licensing and Supervisory Agency LVV has urged Google’s company Tuike Finland to suspend preparatory work at the planned data centers in Muhos and Kajaani. Municipalities in Sweden and Norway negotiating with data center operators can use Amazon’s new line as a reference when they demand transparency.

Source: Data Center Dynamics, TechCrunch, LVV, Verkkouutiset

item.title: IonQ reaches over 1,000 entanglements per second between ion trap and quantum memory – the company’s own record claim
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
IonQ announced on October 9 that it has achieved more than 1,000 entanglement events per second between a qubit in an ion trap and a solid-state quantum memory, a so-called silicon-vacancy qubit, connected via photons. The company says this is more than four times faster than the previous trapped-ion record, held by Chris Monroe’s group at Duke University. Monroe is IonQ’s chief scientist, and Duke took part in the new study.

The result is reported in a preprint (arXiv 2610.10705) and is a step toward distributed quantum computing, where several smaller quantum computers are linked together. What has been shown is only the link between a trapped ion and a silicon vacancy. That the architecture works with neutral atoms and superconducting systems, via so-called transducers that convert microwaves to light, is an expectation and has not been demonstrated. The press release lacks figures on fidelity and distance, and “world-first” is IonQ’s own characterization. IonQ is developing the link under DARPA’s HARQ program and has sold systems to the University of Maryland and South Korea’s SDT.

For the Nordics: Several of the largest Nordic quantum projects are built on superconducting qubits, the very platform where IonQ’s link has not yet been shown. Chalmers and the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT) are building a Swedish quantum computer with superconducting circuits, and Finland’s IQM makes superconducting processors. How several such machines can be linked together is therefore relevant here too, but that part remains to be shown.

Source: IonQ, The Quantum Insider, Chalmers (WACQT)

item.title: Mistral launches Large 4 – a trillion-parameter model with open weights promised by the end of October
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 6, Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4, a multimodal model with roughly one trillion parameters, of which 52 billion are active per token. The model is available as a public preview in Mistral Studio, and the company promises to release the weights by the end of the month.

Mistral says the model was trained from scratch on 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own data centers in Europe. Pricing is $1.36 per million input tokens and $4.18 per million output tokens. The performance figures come from Mistral itself: 82 percent on a test in which vulnerabilities must be reproduced and patched, and 61.7 percent on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark. In a human coding evaluation from Surge AI, the model ranks second of five, behind Claude Opus 5. The license is not stated. According to TechCrunch, the launch follows French President Macron’s talk of “a third way in AI,” and Mistral positions the model as an alternative both to closed models and to open models that often come from China.

For the Nordics: since February, Mistral has said it is investing €1.2 billion in AI data centers in Sweden together with EcoDataCenter, with the facility planned to open in 2027. It is not yet clear whether Large 4 will run there. Open weights would let banks such as SEB and DNB, and public agencies, run the model on their own infrastructure, which matters to IMY and Datatilsynet when personal data must be kept within the EU/EEA and under the organization’s own control. The license terms will decide how far that goes.

Source: Mistral AI, TechCrunch, VKTR

item.title: Norway’s government and the social partners sign a letter of intent on responsible AI at work
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 2, the Norwegian government and the social partners signed a letter of intent on the responsible introduction and use of AI in working life. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Minister of Digitalisation Torgeir Micaelsen sat down with NHO, KS, Virke and Spekter on the employer side and LO, Unio, Akademikerne and YS on the employee side.

The agreement is meant to base the introduction of AI on the Norwegian working-life model, and the parties share responsibility for using existing laws and agreements so that AI is introduced safely and fairly. A coordination group with all the parties will prioritize topics and organize the work. Micaelsen says AI must not become a technology that people fear and avoid using, and that Norway and Europe should develop more language models of their own alongside commercial ones. On October 5, digi.no reported that the government will replace the first national AI strategy, from 2020, with a new one, expected in the first half of 2027.

For the Nordics: the agreement covers Norwegian working life, but the three-party model, with the state, NHO and LO at the same table, offers a point of comparison for Sweden, where the corresponding parties include Svenskt Näringsliv, LO, TCO and Saco. It is a statement of intent, and the sources reviewed contain no binding rules or deadlines. Micaelsen says the rapid development of advanced AI models challenges security, privacy and safety in new ways; for privacy matters, Datatilsynet is the supervisory authority.

Source: Regjeringen.no, digi.no, digi.no (AI-strategin)

item.title: Anthropic updates its usage policy – bans sustained, pointless cruelty toward Claude
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 8, Anthropic published an updated usage policy that takes effect on November 12. Among the changes is a ban on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward the company’s models.

According to Anthropic the ban applies only to extreme cases in which users repeatedly act cruelly with no discernible purpose, not to ordinary frustration, pushback, dark creative themes or testing. Claude can already end conversations with persistently harmful or abusive users, and that remains the main enforcement tool. The policy also gets a consolidated section on deceptive campaigns, such as fake accounts and fabricated news sites. The elections section is narrowed to deceiving voters or disrupting elections, and the earlier blanket ban on personalized vote and campaign targeting is removed. The weapons ban now explicitly covers guidance and control software for weapons, including arming drones and other autonomous vehicles, and Claude may not be used to decide or recommend who should be investigated, arrested or charged.

For the Nordics: the rules apply to all users in the region from November 12. The clarification on weapons software and autonomous vehicles matters for the defense industry, where companies such as Saab and Kongsberg build systems with AI components; how the line will be drawn in practice is an open question. The ban on letting Claude decide who is investigated or charged is a limit that agencies such as Polismyndigheten and Kripos need to be aware of if they use the model. Computer Sweden reported on the ban on cruelty toward Claude on October 9.

Source: Anthropic, TechCrunch, Computer Sweden

item.title: Uber and Pony.ai to test robotaxis in London within weeks
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Uber and China’s Pony.ai plan to begin testing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis in London within weeks. The companies describe it as a test effort and have not announced a timetable for passenger service.

The expansion is part of a partnership that in August set a target of deploying more than 2,000 Pony.ai robotaxis in Europe. The setup follows the Zagreb model, where Pony.ai supplies the driving system and vehicles, Croatia’s Verne owns and operates the fleet, and Uber provides access to its ride-hailing platform. Who will own and operate the fleet in London has not been said. Since September 3, Uber has also offered supervised autonomous rides in London with the British company Wayve, with a driver on board. The UK has opened applications for small-scale pilots of automated passenger services, ahead of a full permitting regime expected in the second half of 2027.

For the Nordics: no Nordic companies are mentioned in the reporting on the London plans. It is an open question how quickly Transportstyrelsen in Sweden and Statens vegvesen in Norway can grant comparable permits for trials, and whether Nordic carmakers such as Volvo Cars become suppliers or competitors to Chinese systems like Pony.ai’s in Europe. Chinese systems on European roads could also raise questions about data flows, an area where IMY and Datatilsynet are supervisory authorities.

Source: TechCrunch, RuntimeWire

item.title: Schneider Electric to buy PTC for $22.6 billion – building on Norway’s Cognite
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 5, Schneider Electric agreed to buy software maker PTC in an all-cash deal at $205 per share. That values PTC’s equity at about $22.6 billion, and the boards of both companies have unanimously approved the deal.

Schneider justifies the deal with industrial AI: PTC’s engineering data is to be linked with operational data so that AI agents get the context they need. The group already owns AVEVA and agreed in June to buy Cognite at an enterprise value of $3.1 billion. CEO Olivier Blum speaks of a digital thread for the next generation of industrial AI. The deal requires approval from PTC shareholders and regulators and is expected to close by the third quarter of 2027.

For the Nordics: Cognite is a Norwegian software company focused on industrial AI, and Aker, TCV and Accel are among the sellers. Schneider’s combination of AVEVA, Cognite and PTC could affect how much of Nordic industry’s data and design tooling ends up with a single supplier. That matters to industrial groups such as AB Volvo, Saab and Kongsberg as they choose platforms for industrial AI, and it is an open question for competition authorities, including Norway’s Konkurransetilsynet.

Source: Robotics 24/7, Houthoff

item.title: Google launches a universal Gemini agent for work – aimed at enterprise customers
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 8, at Gemini at Work 2026, Google presented a Gemini agent that the company calls a universal agent for work. The agent starts from a single prompt box and is meant to handle knowledge work, question answering, content creation and coding.

According to Google, the agent has access to all of an organization's business context, plans the work, uses skills and tools and connects to Cloud customers' business systems. Finished output is delivered in the document, email and developer environments users already work in. The agent picks a suitable model for each task and has built-in cost controls. Google says it has the security, administration and governance that enterprise customers require, but gives no detail, price or availability. The launch comes eight days after Gemini 4 Argon, which was released on September 30.

For the Nordics: price and regional availability are not yet known, so it is too early to say what the agent means for Nordic companies. Google's statement on administration and governance leaves open which rules apply for banks such as SEB and DNB and industrial groups such as Volvo and Ericsson. An agent that reaches business systems and writes in email and documents also raises new questions for IMY and Datatilsynet about which personal data flows where.

Source: Google Cloud, Bloomberg

item.title: Anthropic launches an AI program to protect critical infrastructure – plus a free code scanner for open source
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 8, Anthropic presented the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, which gives security providers access to the company's frontier models, on-site engineers and threat research to protect operational technology (OT) behind power grids, water systems and transport networks, and government systems. The program starts with a small cohort of providers.

Eleven founding partners are on board: Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Alongside it comes OSS Scanner, an opt-in, free service in which open-source projects that sign up receive periodic scans from Anthropic's most capable models. Each finding comes with a proof of concept, an explanation and, where available, a suggested fix. The reports are model-generated and sent without human review, so some may contain errors, for example in severity ratings; Anthropic expects a true-positive rate above 90 percent. Axios notes that it is unclear how partners will test and deploy fixes without disrupting utility operations, and that Anthropic has not said whether partners get free model access or who pays the compute costs. Project Glasswing was earlier in the week merged into an expanded Cyber Verification Program.

For the Nordics: none of the eleven founding partners is headquartered in the Nordic region, but Accenture, Deloitte and PwC operate there. The kind of operational technology the program targets is found at Nordic grid owners, waterworks and industrial groups, and Anthropic says more partners and sectors will follow. It is an open question whether players such as Svenska kraftnät, Statnett and the Swedish Civil Defence Authority (MCF) will be part of the program, and how it relates to the NIS2 incident-reporting requirements.

Source: Anthropic, Axios

item.title: Chalmers has built an AI scientist that sets hypotheses, runs experiments and learns from the results
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology, the University of Gothenburg and the University of Cambridge have built an AI system that formulates biological questions, proposes experiments, evaluates the results and uses them in the next step, in a closed feedback loop. Chalmers published the news on September 30.

The system was tested in systems biology on yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and was given extensive information on the organism's genome, metabolism and earlier research as its knowledge base. It builds on large language models and automated reasoning, linked to a laboratory component in which lab results steer the next experiment. The work builds on Ross King's earlier robot scientists Adam and Eve, and the study, Agentic AI integrated with scientific knowledge: laboratory validation in systems biology, is published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface. The researchers stress that the system is not meant to replace people: Ross King says humans still set research priorities, interpret the wider scientific significance and ensure ethical oversight. Chalmers does not report how many hypotheses were generated or confirmed.

For the Nordics: the work is funded by the Wallenberg program WASP, the UK's EPSRC, the Chalmers AI Research Centre (CHAIR) and Formas, and is an example of Swedish AI research moving from decision support toward systems that produce knowledge themselves. When a system proposes and runs experiments, the question for institutions such as Chalmers, the University of Gothenburg, KTH and Karolinska Institutet is how results are to be reviewed and credited, and how much lab work in Swedish biotech and drug research such a loop could eventually take over.

Source: Chalmers, Evertiq

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 with Intelligent UI – ChatGPT answers with buttons, charts and calculators
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
OpenAI began rolling out Intelligent UI in ChatGPT on October 7, together with a new GPT-6 model. The feature lets ChatGPT present parts of its answers as interactive elements, such as tappable buttons, task-specific calculators and editable charts and graphs. Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users got access on October 7, and users of the free tier and the Go tier followed on October 8.

According to OpenAI's internal tests, as reported by TechStartups, GPT-6 Instant starts answering web-search questions 44 percent sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant. The measure is when the answer begins to appear, not when it is finished. GPT-6 Extra High begins responding at about the same speed as GPT-5.6 Medium. According to TechStartups, paid tiers get GPT-6 Sol and free tiers get GPT-6 Luna, and the change applies only to the chat experience, not to the models in Work and Codex. OpenAI acknowledges that Intelligent UI is still a work in progress, especially in how the system chooses layouts and interactive elements, and ChatGPT has more than 1.2 billion weekly users according to TechStartups. The speed figures come from OpenAI; independent measurements are missing.

For the Nordics: in the Enterprise version, workplace administrators control access according to TechStartups, so it is Nordic companies and public bodies that decide for themselves whether to switch the feature on. For organisations under GDPR, such as banks like SEB and DNB and the public sector, it is an open question whether interactive elements generated in the conversation affect what data leaves the organisation. OpenAI has not addressed it in the sources we reviewed, and we have not found any assessment from IMY or Datatilsynet.

Source: TechCrunch, TechStartups

item.title: DNB cuts about 400 FTEs in its technology division – and names AI as the driver itself
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
DNB announced on October 6 at 09:00 in a stock exchange release that staffing in the Technology & Services division will fall by about 400 full-time equivalents (FTEs). The bank itself states that agentic AI has been introduced in several parts of the business and that AI agents can deliver substantial efficiency gains, with customer data control, KYC work, and technology development and coding as examples. That is the bank's own wording, not an outside interpretation. Group CEO Kjerstin Braathen says AI is changing how the bank works and how it delivers services to its customers.

The figure is FTEs, not employees, and applies only to Technology & Services, not the whole bank. At the end of 2025 the group had 10,603 FTEs and 11,649 employees according to its annual report, so 400 FTEs is just under 4 percent of FTEs. The downsizing is to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026, while the full cost effect will show in the accounts only from the second quarter of 2027; no cost figure has been published. DNB has not reported any quantified AI gain and has not broken down the FTEs by function, so how much of the reduction AI explains is unreported. AI is also one of several rationales; the bank also cites better customer experiences, greater efficiency and customers' future needs. Whether this will mean dismissals or voluntary solutions has not been determined by the bank; the process is to follow applicable rules and take place in close dialogue with employee representatives. Finansforbundet deputy leader Arne Fredrik Håstein criticises the pace in E24: he warns against making AI a law of nature that automatically means fewer employees, and says all options for staff must be explored before anyone is dismissed.

For the Nordics: the sequence is sharp. On October 2 the Norwegian government and the social partners signed an agreement on responsible AI in working life, and four days later DNB announced 400 FTEs would go, with AI as the stated driver. Whether the agreement is meant to cover a case like this is an open question, and events following one another in time are not the same as cause and effect. For Sweden, the DNB announcement becomes a reference point that SEB, Nordea and Finansförbundet can compare against. The EU AI Act regulates AI systems and their use, not individual staffing decisions.

Source: DNB, E24, Norwegian government

item.title: TSMC's September revenue up 54.6 percent – but slightly below August
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On October 8, TSMC reported consolidated revenue of about NT$511.86 billion for September 2026. That is 54.6 percent more than in September 2025 but 0.6 percent less than in August. For the first nine months of the year, revenue came to about NT$3,898.7 billion, an increase of 41.1 percent over the same period in 2025.

August stood at NT$514.81 billion, so the September figure is a marginal month-on-month decline. The revenue report does not break out how much comes from AI chips, so the link to AI demand is the trade press's interpretation and not something TSMC reports in the monthly release. Monthly figures are also a rough indicator: revenue is affected by delivery timing and exchange rates, and the quarterly report gives a fuller picture.

For the Nordics: the Nordic data-centre build-outs rest on the same manufacturing chain. Stargate Norway at Kvandal outside Narvik, to be owned by a joint venture between Nscale and Aker, is an example of an investment where the supply of AI chips affects how quickly capacity can be brought online; Nvidia's chips are, by general account, largely made by TSMC. A continued high TSMC figure says nothing about Nordic delivery times specifically, but it shows that demand for the manufacturing has not abated.

Source: TSMC (september), TSMC (augusti)

item.title: Anthropic releases Haiku 5.5 – a small model at a tenth of its predecessor's input price
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7. The model costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, against $1 and $5 for Haiku 4.5. According to Anthropic it is the company's cheapest, fastest and most capable small model, and it is available on AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.

In Anthropic's own table, Haiku 5.5 scores 72.4 percent on OSWorld 2.1 (an offline subset), against 15.7 for Haiku 4.5 and 48.9 for OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, and 45.9 percent on Humanity's Last Exam without tools. Sonnet 5.5 scores higher on both, at 83.9 and 56.9 percent. The company says Haiku 5.5 is on average about 75 percent cheaper to run than Haiku 4.5 (90 percent for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, 50 percent above that), and that the price of cache reads on Sonnet 5.5 has been halved from $0.20 to $0.10 per million tokens. All figures come from Anthropic and its customers, among them Asana, HubSpot and Box; independent measurements are still missing.

For the Nordics: a token price this low can make it economical to run small models at high volume, for example ticket triage, document reading and background steps in agents. That matters for Nordic software companies and IT consultancies building on Claude, such as Stockholm-based Lovable, and for banks and insurers such as SEB and DNB, where the volume of routine work is large. The price does not change data protection, however: IMY and Datatilsynet apply the same requirements to the handling of personal data regardless of model size.

Source: Anthropic

item.title: Finland orders Google to halt groundwork at two data centre sites
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Finland's permitting and supervisory authority LVV on October 6 ordered Google's Finnish project company Tuike Finland to stop preparatory groundwork at the planned data centres in Muhos and Kajaani. The halt must take effect immediately and no later than October 23, and last until the environmental impact assessments are complete. The company must respond in writing by October 14.

The halt covers tree felling, topsoil removal, excavation, blasting and crushing as well as site roads and storage areas, but not planning, measurements or soil surveys. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation says more than 300 hectares of forest were cleared in Muhos, roughly 420 football pitches, before the impact assessment was complete. Google says it acted in good faith under the Forest Act, but has said it did not meet the high standards it sets itself and that it will comply. Otherwise the authority is considering enforcement, which can be backed by a conditional fine. The projects are part of a EUR 13 billion Finnish investment that Google calls its largest in Europe.

For the Nordics: the case is Finnish but the question is Nordic. A supervisory authority is stopping a hyperscale build during preparation, not once the building stands, and it is Google's communications manager for Finland and Norway, Sondre Ronander, who has answered for the company. Municipalities courting data centres, in Sweden for example Luleå and in Norway Skien, get a fresh example that clearing and groundwork can be halted before the environmental assessment is finished. It is a natural question for permitting authorities and municipalities in both countries: in what order do assessment and groundwork happen here?

Source: LVV, Helsinki Times, AFP/The Star

item.title: OpenAI publishes 722 maths manuscripts – the results are not yet independently reviewed
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
In early October OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts on GitHub with solutions or progress on 372 major mathematical problems, produced by an as yet unreleased internal model. According to OpenAI nearly every manuscript came from a single prompt to a single AI agent, and the average result required about three hours of ChatGPT Pro use.

OpenAI's claims include a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and progress toward the Riemann hypothesis. The advisory group of mathematicians AGMAI is linked to the release, but the results still have to be assessed by mathematicians, and scepticism persists after the earlier dispute over the Navier–Stokes claim. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland says claims of single-prompt solutions should be treated as unverified until the model is released and the results can be replicated. OpenAI has disclosed the model's reasoning and estimates of compute, but withholds the prompts and the compute time per problem.

For the Nordics: the Abel Prize is awarded by the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters in Oslo, and the mathematics departments at KTH, Chalmers, NTNU and the University of Oslo, among others, face the same question as colleagues abroad: how do you assess hundreds of machine-written proofs that nobody has had time to read? The Swedish Research Council and the Research Council of Norway may need clear guidelines for how AI-generated proofs are reviewed before they count as results. A first test will be which of the 722 manuscripts a Nordic research group can actually verify.

Source: Engadget, Scientific American

item.title: Anthropic launches Sonnet 5.5 – a faster model at the same price as its predecessor
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28. According to the company, the model is more than 30 percent faster in output speed than the previous generation and costs the same as Sonnet 5: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Anthropic says the cost per task falls by up to 30 percent, mainly because the model uses fewer tokens and fewer tool calls, not because of a lower list price. On GDPval-AA, a test of occupational tasks, Sonnet 5.5 scores 1,844 against 1,846 for Opus 5.5, and it reaches 70.6 percent on the coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0. The figures come from the company and its customers; independent measurements are not yet available. Haiku 5.5 is promised within weeks.

For the Nordics: Stockholm-based Lovable is among the customers cited – in its tests the number of tool calls fell by about a third and shell executions by roughly half. Because the list price is unchanged, it is the efficiency gain rather than a price cut that shapes the calculation for Nordic software companies and IT consultancies building agents on Claude. The model is available through AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, so Nordic organizations can buy it through cloud agreements they already have.

Source: SiliconANGLE, VentureBeat

item.title: OpenAI watermarks ChatGPT text in the EU ahead of the AI Act labelling deadline
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
OpenAI announced on October 5 that text from ChatGPT and Codex in the EU is to be marked over the coming weeks with textGrain, an invisible statistical watermark built into word choice. In the API the marking is switched off by default and must be enabled per project or organization.

The background is Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act, which requires AI-generated content to be marked in a machine-readable format; systems already on the market before August 2, 2026 must comply by December 2, 2026. According to OpenAI's technical report, the watermark is detected in about 95 percent of 400-token passages but only 17 percent after heavy rewriting, and the detector is initially open only to selected researchers and organizations, including Cornell, ETH Zurich and Slovakia's KInIT. According to ActuIA and Tech Jack Solutions, Anthropic instead applies its marking globally.

For the Nordics: Because the watermark is not on by default in the API, responsibility may fall on Swedish and Norwegian companies building customer-facing services on OpenAI's models – they may need to switch it on themselves before December 2 if the service targets users in the EU. Sweden faces the same deadline, and Norway intends to incorporate the regulation through the EEA Agreement. Whether the obligation sits with the provider or with the Nordic company building the service is something each company must assess for itself.

Source: ActuIA, Tech Jack Solutions

item.title: Norwegian Consumer Council wants AI glasses off the shelves – government plans temporary ban
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
The Norwegian Consumer Council (Forbrukerrådet) has asked the country's optician chains to stop selling glasses with built-in AI until the authorities have clarified what is lawful. Director Finn Myrstad argues that the glasses lay the ground for a surveillance society that most people do not want.

According to BT, Synsam, Brilleland and Interoptik are among the chains selling Ray-Ban Meta glasses; none responded to NTB's questions on Monday, and Specsavers says it does not stock smart glasses. On Monday the government announced a temporary ban on AI glasses in public spaces, schools, kindergartens and other places where children spend time, as well as health institutions, and Digitalisation Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said a bill will go to the Storting as quickly as possible. Sales of Ray-Ban Meta have, according to CNBC as cited by BT, risen from 2 million units in 2023–2024 to over 7 million in 2025.

For the Nordics: Norway is moving ahead of Sweden. In August Karianne Tung, then digitalisation minister, said the government wanted to consider banning facial recognition of others through smart glasses, with an expert group due to advise this autumn; Datatilsynet and the Consumer Council had already called for stricter rules. Any ban must fit within the GDPR, EEA rules and the EU AI Act. We have not found a corresponding proposal in Sweden.

Source: BT, Altaposten, iNyheter

item.title: Half of the applications to the G7–Nordic quantum call include Nordic partners
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
According to Quantum Zeitgeist, citing NordForsk, 93 of the 186 applications submitted to the joint Canada–G7–Nordic call on quantum technologies include Nordic partners, or 50 percent. The Nordic part is administered by NordForsk.

The Nordic budget is up to NOK 84 million, with a maximum of NOK 7 million per project, and the aim is to fund about twelve projects for up to three years. Nordic consortia must include research-performing organizations in at least two Nordic countries. The funders are Innovation Fund Denmark, the Research Council of Finland, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.

For the Nordics: With at most NOK 84 million and about twelve projects, competition will be fierce – roughly one in eight Nordic applications could be funded, by our own calculation from the figures above. The requirement of at least two Nordic countries pushes Nordic collaboration rather than national efforts, with the Swedish Research Council and the Research Council of Norway among the four funders. Which research environments have applied is not stated, and NordForsk does not say in the material we have seen when decisions will be made.

Source: NordForsk, Quantum Zeitgeist

item.title: Aleph Alpha releases Kolibri – an open German-English model with 78 billion parameters
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Germany's Aleph Alpha has released Kolibri, an open-weight model with 78.1 billion parameters in total, of which only 3.46 billion are active per token. The model is licensed under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face, has a context window of just over one million tokens and is trained for German and English.

According to MarkTechPost, the model was trained on 24 trillion tokens, more than 2 trillion of them German, and the company reports an overall score of 75.5 in English and 70.8 in German, plus 84.3 on GPQA Diamond. The figures are the company's own and no independent evaluation has been published; Made With Models notes that they should be read as the company's claims, not as proof. The FP8 version is about 78 GB and, according to MarkTechPost, runs on a single H200, B200 or B300 GPU, or on two H100s.

For the Nordics: Kolibri is trained for German and English, and we have seen no information about Swedish or Norwegian. The model is therefore mainly a point of comparison for AI Sweden and KI Norge at the Norwegian Digitalisation Agency, which build language resources for their own languages, and for Sweden's work on a national Swedish-language model. For regulated businesses such as SEB, DNB and Equinor, the option of running an open model in-house is interesting, but only after their own testing in Swedish and Norwegian.

Source: Aleph Alpha, MarkTechPost, Made With Models

item.title: Reflection AI unveils Beam – an open model with 501 billion parameters, but the weights arrive only later in October
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
US-based Reflection AI unveiled Beam on October 5, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501 billion parameters in total and 23 billion active per token. The model is in final red teaming and is currently available only through a waitlist, with an OpenAI-compatible API.

According to Reflection, the weights will be released under Apache 2.0 later in October, and no pricing has been announced. The company says the model was trained on 23.8 trillion tokens on 6,144 Nvidia GB300 GPUs, that the context window is one million tokens and that the model scores 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified and 80.1 on Terminal Bench v2.1. The figures are the company's own and no independent measurement has been published; the model handles text only.

For the Nordics: Because the weights have not been released, Beam cannot yet be run in-house; it is a promise, not an available model. If they are released under Apache 2.0, organizations that need to run models themselves, such as Ericsson, Telenor, Equinor, SEB and DNB, get a US alternative to the Chinese open models. The European point of comparison is Aleph Alpha's Kolibri. We have seen no information that Nordic companies are testing Beam.

Source: Reflection AI, MarkTechPost

item.title: Breaches at four South Korean banks – AI tools suspected, 25,000 Shinhan customers affected
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Hackers have broken into systems for loan processing, sales support and staff at four South Korean banks, and the worst affected is Shinhan Bank with roughly 25,000 customers, according to the Korea Herald. According to Herald Business, the attacker bypassed identity verification in a mobile service used by loan agents and tried randomized customer numbers over and over to extract the data.

The data includes names, phone numbers, income and loan limits, and at Shinhan also 66 Korean resident registration numbers. Hana Bank (89 customers), KB Kookmin (119) and BNK (11 records on contract staff) are affected on a smaller scale. That AI was used is a suspicion, not confirmed: security analysts told the Korea Herald they found traces of an AI penetration-testing tool, ARTEX AI, on a server suspected of being linked to the Shinhan attack, but the authorities have not confirmed it. The Financial Services Commission (FSC) held an emergency meeting on October 2 and called for checks of externally accessible systems, stronger authentication, tighter access controls and faster sharing of threat information.

For the Nordics: We have seen nothing to suggest that Nordic banks are affected. For Finansinspektionen in Sweden and Finanstilsynet in Norway, the practical question is whether today's requirements for security testing and incident reporting are enough when an attacker uses AI to automate the search for weaknesses. The case also shows that the Shinhan breach came through an ancillary service for loan agents and not through the bank's core systems.

Source: Korea Herald, Herald Business, Insurance Journal
